name: Solenne Atelier Ossuary Couture Veil Coat
description: A singular piece by Solenne Atelier's lead designer Ifeoma Vasić-Nakamura, constructed over eight months from cultured bone-lace panels grown in a biolab and laser-cut into interlocking geometric screens. The silhouette is an oversized cocoon coat that falls to the ankle, the bone-lace layered over a base of liquid-black nanosilk that shifts between opacity and translucency based on ambient temperature. The collar rises into a structured halo frame supporting a detachable veil of graphene-mesh so fine it reads as smoke. Wrist closures are hand-set with reclaimed antique jet beads from pre-Collapse Edo-era jewelry. One of three made.
functionality: Nanosilk layer provides passive thermal regulation. Graphene veil filters 40% of particulate air pollution. Bone-lace panels are structurally reinforced — surprisingly impact-resistant for haute couture.
what_it_says: This person exists at a level where clothing is no longer about function or even status — it is about authorship.
worn_by: one known to be owned by a sitting Crucible board member
story_hooks: One of the three coats has gone missing from a private auction — the designer is quietly frantic, the buyer is not yet aware.
A journalist discovers the 'cultured bone-lace' was grown from genetic material sourced without consent from Shelf-tier residents used in a biolab study.
Wearing this coat to a particular Spire gathering is understood as a declaration of alliance with a specific corponation faction — the wearer may not know this.

physical_description.visual_profile: A haunting, architectural silhouette that reads as equal parts funeral rite and haute couture—an oversized cocoon that drapes to the ankle with an ethereal, almost spectral presence. The bone-lace panels create an intricate lattice effect that suggests both anatomical fragility and geometric precision. The rising halo collar frames the face with ceremonial formality, while the graphene veil catches light like suspended smoke.
physical_description.fit: Dramatically oversized cocoon silhouette; relaxed through the body with architectural volume, structured only at the collar and cuffs. Designed to obscure the wearer's form while commanding visual space.
physical_description.primary_material: Cultured bone-lace panels (biolab-grown, laser-cut) layered over liquid-black nanosilk base with temperature-responsive opacity. Graphene-mesh veil. Reclaimed Edo-era jet beads.
physical_description.texture: Bone-lace creates a delicate, skeletal filigree with sharp geometric edges; nanosilk beneath is smooth and fluid. The graphene veil is impossibly fine—nearly invisible but tactile. Jet beads add occasional hard, smooth focal points at the wrists.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary liquid-black with cream/ivory bone-lace lattice creating high contrast. Jet beads read as deep charcoal. The veil shifts between translucent and reflective depending on light and movement.
physical_description.closures: Hand-set jet bead closures at the wrists; the veil is detachable (likely magnetic or friction-fitted to the halo frame). The coat itself appears to be a slip-on cocoon with no visible fasteners—held by its own structured weight and fit.
distinctive_features: Interlocking geometric bone-lace panels grown and laser-cut in biolab
Temperature-responsive nanosilk base (opacity shifts with ambient heat)
Hand-set reclaimed Edo-era jet bead wrist closures
One of only three pieces ever made
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 1 ultra-luxury; Spire-tier couture. This is a statement piece for the highest echelon of GLMZ society.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing this signals deep wealth, avant-garde sensibility, and connection to legacy fashion houses. The bone-lace and funeral-rite aesthetic suggest intellectual engagement with mortality and human fragility—the wearer is cultured, philosophical, and unafraid of dark beauty. The Edo-era beads nod to pre-Collapse heritage and global high culture.
physical_description.condition_typical: Pristine when worn; each wearing is a curation event. The piece is likely stored in climate-controlled archival conditions between appearances.
